bib.title: Small Language Models are the Future of Agentic AI

question: Should the language models inside agentic systems be small language models rather than generalist LLMs?
hypothesis: SLMs are sufficiently powerful (V1), more operationally suitable (V2) and more economical (V3) for most agentic LM invocations, so they are the future of agentic AI, with LLMs used selectively in heterogeneous systems.
contributions: A position statement with three views V1-V3 and seven supporting arguments A1-A7 (Sections 2-3)
A list of adoption barriers B1-B3 (Section 5)
A six-step LLM-to-SLM agent conversion algorithm (Section 6)
Three case studies estimating the share of replaceable LLM queries in MetaGPT, Open Operator and Cradle (Appendix B)

limits: Position paper: no experiment, benchmark run or cost measurement of its own; every capability and efficiency number is borrowed from model reports, blogs or surveys.
The 40-70% replaceability figures in Appendix B are author estimates from reading three open-source agents, with no traces, accuracy or cost data.
The authors acknowledge that the economic view AV2 (centralised LLM inference is cheaper at scale) is valid and case-specific and say 'the jury is still out'.
The authors give no timeline for barriers B1-B3 to fall.
Vision-language models are not considered explicitly.
Several cited capability claims come from NVIDIA's own models (Hymba, Nemotron-H), and the authors are NVIDIA researchers; the paper states views are the authors' own.
The conversion algorithm is described, not validated.
practices: Default to SLMs and invoke LLMs selectively in heterogeneous agent systems (Section 2.3).
Log all non-HCI agent calls (prompts, responses, tool calls, optional latency) in encrypted pipelines with role-based access and anonymisation (S1).
Curate and filter logged data, removing PII/PHI; paraphrase sensitive application inputs; 10k-100k examples as a rule of thumb (S2).
Cluster prompts and agent actions into recurring tasks such as intent recognition, extraction, summarisation, tool-specific code generation (S3).
Select candidate SLMs per task by capability, benchmark performance, licence and deployment footprint (S4).
Fine-tune specialists with LoRA or QLoRA, full fine-tuning if needed, optionally distilling from the generalist LLM (S5).
Retrain SLMs and the router periodically with new data in a continuous loop (S6).
Enforce a single output or tool-call format in post-training so the code parts of an agent get predictable output (A5).

terms.definition: A SLM is a LM that can fit onto a common consumer electronic device and perform inference with latency sufficiently low to be practical when serving the agentic requests of one user.
An LLM is a LM that is not a SLM.
The language model acts both as the HCI and the orchestrator of tool calls to carry out a task.
The language model fills the role of the HCI (optionally) while a dedicated controller code orchestrates all interactions.
Agents invoking multiple different models; SLMs by default, LLMs invoked selectively and sparingly.
